Breakfast at the hotel. Departure at 07:30.

Taboga is in the Gulf of Panama, 12 nautical miles from Panama City. The ferry takes about 30 minutes each way.

Spend the day by the Pacific. The calm water is good for swimming and kayaking, and snorkellers can look for corals and molluscs. Taboga is also worth exploring on foot. Its narrow colonial-era streets pass places linked to well-known people who used to come to the island for a break from the capital.

Island restaurants serve meals, ice cream and drinks.

The day includes return ferry tickets, free Wi-Fi on board and a one-hour history tour with an English- or Spanish-speaking guide.

Lunch is included. Choose between fish in garlic sauce and Creole-style chicken, served with coconut rice, salad, dessert and one alcoholic or non-alcoholic drink.

A sun lounger and beach umbrella are provided. Showers and toilets are available, and a mask and snorkel are provided for snorkelling.

Return to Panama City by ferry and transfer to the hotel.
Colourful waterfront houses and a green hill on Taboga Island, Panama
Taboga, Panama: a sandy bay beside a village on a wooded hillside
Soberanía, Gatún Lake, Fort San Lorenzo and the Agua Clara Locks

Breakfast at the hotel. Depart at 08:00 for Soberanía National Park, home to the village of Gamboa.

First, take a boat along the Chagres River and out into the Panama Canal, where ocean-going ships pass nearby. The boat approaches islands where you may see capuchins, howler monkeys and tamarins in the wild. Crocodiles and turtles are also found here, and with a lot of luck you may spot a manatee.

After returning to the dock, continue to Panama's Caribbean coast. Wild beaches, islands and bays sit alongside places tied to the history of the conquistadors and pirate raids. The forts of San Lorenzo and Portobelo are linked to Francis Drake, Henry Morgan, Edward Vernon and other raiders.

To defend against pirates, King Philip II of Spain ordered a series of forts built along the Caribbean coast, including San Lorenzo, San Jerónimo, Santiago de la Gloria, San Fernando and San Fernandín. In 1980, UNESCO added Panama's 17th- and 18th-century colonial buildings and forts on the Caribbean coast to the World Heritage List.

You'll also visit the Agua Clara Locks on the Caribbean side of the Panama Canal. They opened on 26 June 2016 and handle large Panamax and Neopanamax ships.

The three chambers work on the same principle as the older locks, raising or lowering ships by 26 metres relative to sea level. The visitor centre sits on a bluff with a clear view of passing ships. There are viewing telescopes, and you can see Gatún Lake and ships waiting to enter the canal. The centre also screens a film about the construction of the locks.

Return to Panama City by car. The drive takes about two hours.
